Periyar Nature Preserve There is no crumbly frozen cake to thaw. Today, we are in the jungle. I mean mosquito. I mean tigers and elephants sludging their way to the lake for a drink and Don’t make sudden moves or snakes startled from an afternoon nap will greet you fang first. I think we are lost. Too hot for any cold confection to survive. Even my tube of sunblock is as warm as a baby’s bottle. You get to those places I can’t reach, those places I dared not even whisper before I walked down the aisle in white. You never worried if our families would clash, if they would clang like the clutch of pale monkeys clanging the thin branches of the treetrops, begging for our trail mix. You never worried about my relatives staring at your pale, muscled calves— things not usually seen outside of the bedroom. You wore hiking shorts anyway. And still, they lavished ladle-fuls of food on your plate. I think we are lost. My eyes are dark and wet as that wild deer that walked right past us, a little off the trail. I think we are lost, but for once I don't mind. Eventually you turn us back to a place not on any map, but I know I can trace it back with my finger if we ever need it again. We made it one year without a compass and we’re not about to start now.

# Periyar Nature Preserve

There is no crumbly frozen cake to thaw. Today, we are in the jungle. I mean the mosquitoes. I mean the tigers and elephants, sludging their way to the lake for a drink, and *don't make sudden moves*, or snakes startled from an afternoon nap will greet you fang-first. I think we are lost. It's too hot for any cold confection to survive—even my tube of sunblock feels as warm as a baby's bottle.

You reach the places I cannot, the places I dared not even whisper before I walked down the aisle in white. You never worried whether our families would clash, whether they'd clang together like that troop of pale monkeys rattling the thin treetop branches, begging for our trail mix. You never worried about my relatives staring at your pale, muscled calves—things not usually glimpsed outside the bedroom. You wore your hiking shorts anyway. And still, they lavished ladle-fuls of food onto your plate.

I think we are lost. My eyes are dark and wet as that wild deer's, the one that wandered past us, just off the trail. I think we are lost, but for once, I don't mind.

Eventually, you turn us back toward a place that exists on no map—though I know I could trace it with my finger if we ever needed to find it again. We made it one year without a compass, and we're not about to start using one now.

**Periyar Nature Preserve**

No crumbling icy dessert waits to melt here. Today we're surrounded by wilderness. Or rather, mosquitoes. Or rather, tigers and elephants trudging through mud toward the water's edge, and warnings not to move too quickly or the snakes—jolted awake from their midday rest—might strike before we see them coming. I believe we've lost our way. The heat is too fierce for any frozen treat to survive it. Even my sunscreen has grown as warm as heated milk for an infant.

You reach the places I cannot access myself, the spots I never dared mention aloud until after I'd worn white down that aisle toward you. It never crossed your mind to worry whether our two families might collide, might rattle against each other the way that troop of pale-furred monkeys rattled the slender branches above us, hoping for scraps of our snacks. You never fretted over my relatives' eyes landing on your fair, sculpted legs—the kind of sight typically reserved for private moments. Yet you wore those hiking shorts regardless. And still, they heaped spoonful after spoonful of food onto your plate.

I believe we've lost our way. My eyes have gone dark and glistening like that untamed deer who wandered past us, just beyond the marked path. I believe we've lost our way, though for once, I find I don't care. Eventually you guide us back toward a location no map contains, yet I know my finger could retrace the route should we ever need to find it again. We survived twelve months without a compass, and there's no reason to start relying on one now.

# Into the Periyar: A Journey of Trust and Discovery

The heat presses down like a living thing as the speaker and their partner make their way through the Periyar jungle, where every rustle in the undergrowth might announce a tiger's presence, where elephants move like slow-shifting mountains through the trees, and where snakes coil unseen in the humid shadows. This is not a gentle landscape—it demands vigilance, courage, and above all, trust in one's companion.

It is this very trust that becomes the poem's central metaphor. Just as the couple ventures deeper into unfamiliar, potentially dangerous territory, so too does their physical and emotional intimacy expand into places once unspoken. The speaker reflects that their partner now reaches parts of them—both literal and figurative—that were never acknowledged, never even mentioned, before marriage sanctified this closeness. The jungle becomes a mirror for the private wilderness of a new marriage: uncharted, thrilling, and requiring faith that one's partner will not lead one astray.

What stands out most vividly is the partner's unshaken calm in the face of complications that might unsettle another. He carries no anxiety about the friction that often accompanies two families, two cultures, merging into one. This ease is captured in a striking image: monkeys clanging noisily in the treetops, mirroring perhaps the chatter and scrutiny of relatives, while those same relatives openly stare at his pale, muscled calves—a foreign, curious sight among them. Yet none of this shakes him. He moves through both the literal jungle and the metaphorical one of cultural difference with the same unbothered assurance.

The speaker, meanwhile, admits to feeling genuinely lost amid the dense foliage and uncertain paths of Periyar. And yet, surprisingly, this disorientation brings not fear but comfort, even joy. In a moment of quiet connection with the wild, the speaker catches sight of a deer just off the trail and recognizes something of themselves in its eyes—alert, watchful, yet unafraid, alive to the strangeness of the moment rather than crushed by it.

The poem draws to a close with a tender meditation on the couple's first year together. Despite having no compass, no clear map to guide them through either the literal jungle or the metaphorical terrain of a new marriage, they have managed to find their way. There is a quiet confidence in the closing lines: even without instruments to measure their direction, they trust that they could retrace their steps if they needed to—a testament to how deeply they have already come to know and rely upon one another.

# Lost and Found in Periyar

The heat presses down like a hand on the chest as they push deeper into Periyar's green throat, leaves slapping wet against bare arms, the trail more suggestion than certainty beneath their feet. Somewhere ahead, or perhaps behind, elephants trumpet through the canopy—a sound that seems to come from everywhere and nowhere, much like the doubts that crept into their marriage during its first uncertain months.

She walks ahead, machete-quiet, reading signs he cannot see: a broken branch, a print in mud, the particular silence that means something large is near. He follows, sweat-soaked and grateful, thinking of her mother's kitchen back home, the spices whose names he still mispronounces, the prayers he mouths silently at gatherings, unsure of the words but sure of his place beside her.

"We're lost," she says, not for the first time, laughing despite the sun blazing directly overhead, despite the map that makes no sense in this humidity, despite eleven months of marriage that sometimes feels like navigating without instruments. He thinks of his own family's gatherings—the different rhythms of conversation, the unfamiliar customs she's learning to inhabit, the small collisions of two worlds trying to become one.

The path disappears entirely near a stream crossing, stones slick with algae, and they stand debating which way leads back to camp. This is marriage, he thinks: two people from different maps, different languages of love, trying to read the same impossible terrain. Her family speaks in one cultural tongue, his in another, and between them they are constructing a third language, stumbling but persistent, built from patience and translation and the willingness to say *I don't understand, help me see this the way you see it.*

They emerge from the jungle at dusk, mud-streaked, mosquito-bitten, without ever finding the marked trail they'd meant to follow. But they have found something else—a validation more solid than any guidebook could offer. No compass, no map, no fluent guide through this new territory of shared life. Only each other's voices in the growing dark, only trust accumulated step by uncertain step.

"We made it," she says, and it isn't triumph in her voice but something quieter—recognition, perhaps, or the beginning of faith. He takes her hand, still damp from the day's heat, and thinks: if we can find our way here, lost and found in equal measure, we can find our way through anything. The jungle taught them nothing about elephants or orchids or the medicinal properties of local plants, but everything about proceeding without certainty, about trusting instinct over instruction, about becoming, together, each other's only reliable map.
outputs.L5:
# The Periyar Nature Preserve: A Sanctuary of Biodiversity

Nestled in the Western Ghats of Kerala, India, the Periyar Nature Preserve stands as one of the most remarkable ecological treasures in South Asia. Established around the picturesque Periyar Lake, this protected sanctuary spans approximately 925 square kilometers, encompassing a rich tapestry of tropical forests, grasslands, and wetlands that support extraordinary biodiversity.

## A Refuge for Wildlife

The preserve is perhaps best known for its population of Asian elephants, which can often be observed near the lake's shores, particularly during the drier months when they gather to drink and bathe. Beyond elephants, Periyar serves as a critical habitat for the elusive Bengal tiger, as part of India's Project Tiger conservation initiative. The dense forests also shelter Indian bison (gaur), sambar deer, wild boar, and numerous species of primates, including the endangered lion-tailed macaque.

Birdwatchers find Periyar equally captivating, with over 260 bird species recorded within its boundaries, including the great hornbill, Malabar grey hornbill, and various species of kingfishers and eagles.

## Ecological Significance

The Western Ghats, where Periyar is located, represents one of the world's eight "hottest hotspots" of biological diversity. The preserve plays a vital role in protecting this fragile ecosystem, safeguarding countless endemic plant and animal species found nowhere else on Earth. The forests here also serve as an essential watershed, feeding the Periyar River and supporting agricultural communities downstream.

## Balancing Conservation and Tourism

Periyar has pioneered eco-tourism initiatives that involve local communities in conservation efforts. Boat safaris on the lake offer visitors the chance to observe wildlife in their natural habitat while minimizing human disturbance. Trekking programs, often guided by former poachers turned conservationists, demonstrate how sustainable tourism can simultaneously protect biodiversity and provide economic opportunities for local populations.

## Conclusion

The Periyar Nature Preserve exemplifies the delicate balance between conservation and human coexistence. As climate change and habitat loss threaten ecosystems worldwide, sanctuaries like Periyar serve as crucial reminders of nature's resilience and the importance of dedicated conservation efforts in preserving our planet's biological heritage for future generations.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free verse poem about a couple traveling in Periyar Nature Preserve in India, blending themes of marriage, cultural differences, and feeling lost together.
counterfactuals.output:
**Periyar**

The boat pulls away from the dock
and neither of us knows the word
for the bird diving into green water—
you say something in your mother's tongue,
I say something in mine,
and the guide translates us both
into a third language we're still learning
after all these years.

Somewhere past the bamboo groves
an elephant trumpets, unseen,
the sound arriving before we understand
it isn't warning, isn't welcome,
just weather, just a fact of forest.
I reach for your hand
the way I reach for the right word
at your parents' table—
uncertain, hopeful,
willing to be corrected.

The mist here doesn't ask permission.
It simply arrives, erasing
the far shore, the near one,
until we're both just shapes
leaning toward each other
in a boat that smells of diesel
and cardamom and rain.

You point to something in the water—
a shadow, a log, a crocodile maybe—
and I realize this is marriage:
two people squinting at the same thing,
each certain of a different name for it,
each willing to be wrong
in the company of the other.

Later, walking the spice trail,
you'll teach me the word for cinnamon
in a language my mouth
was not built to hold,
and I'll mangle it beautifully,
and you'll laugh the laugh
that made me choose this—
choose the not-knowing,
choose the boat pulling from shore
without a map,
choose getting lost
in a forest that doesn't care
whose passport says what,
whose god goes by which name,

only that we keep moving forward
into the green dark together,
translating the untranslatable
one mistranslated word at a time.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a poem that uses a jungle safari trip as a metaphor for a first wedding anniversary and interracial marriage?
counterfactuals.output:
# One Year Into the Wild

We set out with binoculars and no map,
two travelers from different maps entirely—
you from the coast where the rains come sideways,
me from inland hills that hoard their water jealously.

The guide said: *watch for what surprises you.*
We didn't know we'd be the surprise ourselves,
two different plumages nesting in one tree,
learning the other's calls, their warning cries, their songs of ease.

Twelve months through canopy and clearing.
We forded rivers neither of us named the same—
you called it *creek*, I called it *something wilder*,
and found the water didn't care what language held its frame.

We learned to read each other's weather:
the way you go quiet before a storm of feeling,
the way I circle problems like a cautious cat
before I trust the ground enough for kneeling.

There were nights the jungle pressed in close and foreign,
when my history and yours refused to rhyme—
old griefs that predate us both, inherited compasses
pointing toward different Norths, different notions of time.

But look—we're still here, still walking,
matching stride to stride through green and shadow.
Your hand in mine is not a bridge between two countries.
It's its own country now. It's the only home I know.

A year ago we planted something strange and mixed,
uncertain if the soil would hold, would take.
Today: new growth. Not one thing or the other—
something neither jungle knew before, alive, awake.

The guide was wrong. We didn't watch for wonders.
We *became* the thing worth watching, wild and true—
two separate wildernesses, breathing as one weather,
one strange and sturdy Eden, made of me and you.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the voice of an Indian woman reflecting on her white husband, their honeymoon trip to a wildlife preserve, and family acceptance.
counterfactuals.output:
# Between Two Worlds

My mother said, *are you certain, beti?*
when I brought you home, your hands
so unused to turmeric stains,
your tongue stumbling sweetly
over syllables of my name's true sound.

But you learned. You always learn.

We went to the reserve after the wedding—
red dust settling on your pale arms
like the color was choosing you,
claiming you the way my grandmother's
sari claimed the wind that day
she finally called you *beta*
instead of *him*.

The elephants moved in families, you said,
matriarchs leading, memory
passed down through trunk and tusk—
and I thought of my mother's hands
kneading dough, teaching me
the exact pressure of belonging,
now teaching yours the same.

At dawn we watched a tiger drink
from water that reflected both our faces,
so different, so strangely matched,
and I understood then
how a jungle holds
a thousand kinds of green,
how difference is not division
but a fuller kind of forest.

My father took longer.
Men measure love in different currency—
he watched how you held my hand
in public without shame,
how you tried the language
of my grandmother's stories,
failing, trying again,
until failure itself became
a kind of devotion he could trust.

Now when we visit,
he pours you chai
the way he pours it for his sons,
no separate cup, no careful distance—
just two hands passing warmth
between two men
who learned to see
past the borders
skin was supposed to draw.

The preserve is gone from us now,
just photographs and the memory
of your voice saying *this is home*
while pointing at nothing—
just trees, just sky, just me
standing beside you,
proof that some boundaries
were only ever
lines we agreed to believe.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a narrative poem set in Periyar Nature Preserve that contrasts the wildness of the jungle with the intimacy of a first year of marriage.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Periyar Ledger

They came in the season when the lake ran low,
when the drowned trees stood like grey bones
through the water's skin, and the boat
cut slow between them, engine hushed
so the jungle might forget them, might go on
with its business of hunger and green.

She had been married eleven months.
Long enough to know the particular silence
he carried into rooms, the way he held
his coffee cup with both hands like something
that might otherwise escape him.
Not long enough to stop watching for it.

*Elephant,* the guide whispered, pointing
to where the far bank moved—grey shifting
into grey, ears like torn sails.
A mother and her calf, unbothered,
pulling grass with the deliberate calm
of creatures who have never had to hurry
for anyone's love.

He put his hand over hers on the rail.
This, too, was new: the smallness of gestures
that meant everything, the way a marriage
in its first year is a country
still being mapped—here be the shoals
of his silences, here the warm current
of her laughter, here the places
where the depth suddenly changes
and you must learn to swim.

The jungle did not care for any of this.
It had its own marriages—the fig tree
married to its wasp, the orchid
to the moth that dies pollinating it,
the tiger married to its hunger,
faithful only to that one thing.

That night, in the cottage with its thin walls,
they heard something large move through
the undergrowth—a sambar, maybe,
or worse, and did not speak of it,
only moved closer under the single sheet,
her spine against his chest, his arm
becoming the shape a fence makes
around a small, uncertain field.

*What if we don't know how to do this,*
she'd asked him once, in the city,
months before, in the ordinary dark
of their first apartment.
He hadn't answered. He'd only listened,
the way now they listened together
to the forest's long, indifferent breathing,
the calls of things unseen and unafraid,
the whole wild machinery of survival
turning outside their window
like a world that had already decided
everything it needed to know.

In the morning, mist stood on the lake
like something the water was still deciding
whether to remember. The elephants
had moved on. The boat waited.
They walked down to it together,
not touching, but matched now
in their steps, in the quiet
they had learned to keep between them—
not the silence of separate country,
but the hush two people make
when they have started, finally,
to speak the same rough language
of an untamed and continuing world.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical poem about being "lost" both literally in a nature preserve and metaphorically in love, incorporating imagery of tigers, elephants, and monkeys.
counterfactuals.output:
# Lost in the Green Hour

I took the wrong path at the fork by the fig tree,
the one where you kissed me and called it a compass—
now I can't tell which way leads out of this wanting,
which way leads home.

The preserve swallows maps whole. Somewhere
a tiger moves through amber grass like a rumor,
stripes folding into light the way your name
folds into every sentence I don't mean to speak.
I have been circling this same clearing for an hour,
or a year, or however long
it takes to admit that I am circling *you*—

that thought, orange and burning,
padding soft-footed through my ribs.

The elephants know the way. They always know—
matriarchs humming their low frequencies
through the soles of their feet, remembering
every water hole, every safe crossing
their mothers ever taught them.
I remember the crossing of your hand into mine
at a dinner table years ago, how I knew, even then,
this was a path I'd walk until my feet gave out,
until the water table of my heart ran dry
and still I'd dig.

Above me, monkeys chatter their easy gossip,
swinging from certainty to certainty,
branch to branch, never once
looking down to check if the ground
still exists. I want that kind of faith—
the kind that trusts the next handhold
before it's even seen.
Instead I stand here, lost,
mapless,
trying to read the sun's position
like it might tell me
if you're still thinking of me,
if love is a landmark
or just another kind of wilderness
I wandered into
without a trail guide,
without a flashlight,
following only the sound
of something enormous and quiet
moving invisibly beside me,
the way you move beside me,
unseen, unknown, essential—

a heartbeat in tall grass.
A memory the elephants keep.
A rustle in the highest leaves
that might be laughter,
might be warning,
might just be the wind
learning your name.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
